question: A student elicits pinpoint bleeding from a scaly plaque using a scalpel blade and a single forceful scrape, without first observing silvery flaking or a glistening membrane. How should this result be interpreted?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A true Auspitz sign can only be claimed when it appears as the third and final endpoint of the graded sequence — after the candle-grease sign and glistening membrane — using a blunt instrument and gentle pressure.

answers.text: Unreliable — the bleeding is likely traumatic from sharp, vigorous scraping rather than a true sequential Auspitz sign

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The Grattage test requires a blunt instrument and graded scraping to elicit three endpoints in order. Bleeding produced by a sharp blade and a forceful single scrape bypasses the orderly layers and most likely represents traumatic laceration, not the specific Auspitz sign.

answers.text: A negative Grattage test ruling out psoriasis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. An incorrectly performed test allows no valid conclusion — the technique was flawed, so neither a positive nor a negative result can be drawn from it.
Incorrect. This finding cannot diagnose any specific condition because the technique was fundamentally flawed — a sharp instrument and aggressive scraping invalidate the result entirely.

overallFeedback.feedback: The Grattage test relies on graded scraping with a blunt instrument to reveal three layers in sequence. A sharp blade and forceful scraping produces traumatic bleeding that cannot be reliably distinguished from a true Auspitz sign.
Exactly right. Technique matters: the Auspitz sign is diagnostically meaningful only when it appears as the final endpoint of a properly graded test using a blunt instrument.
